May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he not think that in this house we can only carry on business if, so to speak, we play the game with each other? Then may I ask him whether he does not think that this amendment to do away with this whole item is not a resolution to be taken seriously but is merely for the purpose of causing delay? Coming back to my first question, may I ask the hon. member whether he does not agree that in this house.

if we reach the stage where we are not cooperating with the Speaker, and if we reach the stage where we cannot really co-operate with each other within the rules, we are drifting into a very serious and dangerous position?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. In reply to that question I would say we are drifting into a very serious situation.
It is true that this amendment is only an effort to enable us to accomplish an aim, but this has been the practice over the years in dealing with matters in interim supply which are related. I would suggest that if all the amendments presented to this committee had been voted on this afternoon there would have been very little in the speeches of hon. members and we would not have taken very long to dispose of this subject.
In the amendment we have now moved, what we are interested in discussing is the situation that has developed because of this question of disallowance, and this is only in my opinion a method to enable us to discuss it. I agree with the hon. member that we are coming to a very sad impasse when we have to move amendments which are not really meant and we do not really want to accomplish what the amendment seeks. As I say, it is only a method to enable us to talk about something else.
I honestly think it has been very foolish of us to get into this position of having to move an amendment which we do not want to support as such, because we certainly do not want to eliminate the privy council. It is part of the institution of our parliament, but we wish to have an item before the house which will allow us to discuss something which the privy council is, or was, able to do. It is a matter on which we think wrong action was taken and the amendment is only to enable us to bring it before the house.
I agree we have reached a sad impasse when the Chair is put in the position of having to rule out of order matters which I think are very relevant. In reply to the hon. member's question, I know he is an ardent supporter of parliament and I have read his speeches over the years, but I wish he would talk to the Minister of Finance. If the minister had been more quiet in the first place, this debate would probably have been concluded a long time ago.
Mr. Chairman-
Oh, oh.
Why don't you give your colleagues a chance to vote on this?

If hon. members will give me the floor, I should like to say this is an unusual situation. I should like to say a few words which to me are important, even though they may not be important to my hon. friend directly across from me. Mr. Chairman, if there were a greater understanding of the real meaning of democracy, and if there were a greater application of it, then this session of parliament might be a lot shorter than it appears it will be. There should be a greater understanding between all members and all parties.
Will you allow me this one remark, Mr. Chairman, that if all of us-I mean all parties, government, official opposition and the C.C.F.-would realize our responsibility is not to discuss the past but to work on the present and the future, we would be doing a darned sight better than we have for the people we represent. Unfortunately the government cannot recognize that they are now in government. They have to go back to the past. The opposition cannot recognize that they are not now the government, and now they are in opposition they have to go back. Each and every one of us should say, "Okay, let us put a closure on the past and work for Canada from this day on, recognizing all our responsibilities".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the business is for tomorrow? The leader of the house has already indicated what we will be doing on Monday. I wonder if he could tell the house what the business will be prior to budget day, March 31? That is for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would gladly have given a forecast of the business for next week, and would do so now if we could get some clear indication as to what progress we are likely to make this week. But I confess that at the moment I am not able to state more than I announced last night. We have three items here, interim supply, which we were discussing today, the final supplementary estimates, and the resolution dealing with federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements, which should receive urgent treatment by the House of Commons for the orderly dispatch of the business of the country.
Tomorrow we shall carry on with the order of business that I outlined last night, and if we do not finish interim supply in good time I may have to ask the house to drop that subject and deal with the final supplementary estimates in order that the various payments which have to be made to officials serving the government and the people of Canada can be made promptly, as is the habit, every month.

1.	With what retailers, if any, and at what locations have bonded warehousing arrangements been entered into since June 1, 1957, under the provisions of sections 64 to 79 of the Customs Act to facilitate the sale to tourists of goods on display by sample in retail shops for eventual delivery outside Canada, on a duty free basis?
2.	What warehousing fees are payable respecting each such arrangement?
3.	Are goods sold under such arrangements exempt from Canadian sales tax?
Answer by: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister
of National Revenue):
1.	International Resort Facilities Limited, Lansdowne, Ontario, and Sol Margies Limited, Cobourg, Ontario, are two firms known to be utilizing their facilities for in bond sales to United States tourists. There are however 356 bonded warehouses across Canada, any one of which could be used to handle such sales at retail.
2.	Bonded warehouse licence fees are $50 per annum. In addition, these operators are assessed the normal $2.50 per hour special service fee for the attendance of a customs officer during the period the bonded premises are made accessible to the warehousekeeper.
3.	Goods sold ex-warehouse for export are not subject to customs duties, excise and/or sales taxes.

1.	Was a vessel to be used by the marine institute of the department of youth of the province of Quebec, registered in Canada? If so, on what date?
2.	Was an inspection of this vessel made by inspectors of the Department of Transport?
3.	If so, when was the inspection made and were any repairs or modifications required to meet the departmental requirements, and if so, what was their nature?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transport):
1.	Yes. Motor yacht Torlundy, U.K. registry, transferred to Canadian registry at Quebec on March 11th, 1959. Name of vessel changed to Le St. Barnaby on April 15, 1959, under Canadian registered owners, represented by the hon. the minister of youth, Quebec.
2.	Yes.
3.	Inspection commenced June, 1959, and still in progress. Repairs and modifications required as follows:
Strengthening of hull structure and alterations to the accommodation and general interior. Reconditioning of propulsion machinery. Life saving and fire extinguishing equipment to be brought up to the standard of a marine school training vessel engaged
